sentences.text: It was not treasure and Tomás would like that stated at the top, because when he tells this story people always lean forward at exactly this point and he always has to take it away from them.
It was a dog.

The concrete pad was the floor of a shed that had come down in about 2009, and along the road edge of it the slab had cracked and settled and left a gap about the width of a fist between the concrete and the earth, and under the slab there was a void perhaps a metre across where the ground had washed out.
A dog had gone in after something and could not get back out.
She had been in there four days.
Four days.
Tomás did that arithmetic standing on the concrete with his father's jacket in his hands and it is the only part of the whole business that still gets him.
She had been under there on the Monday, when he cycled past twice and looked at a bird.
She had been under there on the Tuesday and the Wednesday, when he stopped and watched for twelve minutes and decided there was nothing in that corner.
She had been under there on the Thursday morning while he sat on the verge with a notebook and a watch, being pleased with himself about method.

She was a small brown mongrel with a collar and no tag and she was extremely thin and completely silent, which was why nobody walking the road had heard a thing — she had gone past barking days ago and was doing the other thing, the quiet thing, that animals do at the end of it.
It took Tomás, his father, and a neighbour with a crowbar about ninety minutes to get the slab up enough to reach in.
The first twenty minutes were spent establishing that there was anything there at all, because the gap was a fist wide and dark and Tomás's father would not let him put his arm in it.
They got a torch on it.
Then they got a longer torch on it.

Then Tomás lay flat on the concrete with his cheek against it and his eye at the gap for about a minute, in silence, with the two men standing over him, and said, in a voice he did not entirely recognise, "There's a dog." After that it was a matter of levers and swearing.

The slab was thicker than it looked and had reinforcing in it, and they could not lift it, and in the end they did not lift it — they broke the corner off it with a sledge, in stages, going carefully because nobody knew exactly where under there she was.
She did not make a sound the entire time.
Not when the sledge went in.
Not when the corner came away and the light got to her.
Tomás's father put his jacket over her and got her out with both hands, and she weighed, he said afterwards, about as much as a bag of sugar, and she was still trying to wag.
The kestrel was overhead for the first half of it and then was not, and Tomás did not see her go.
He has thought about the bird every so often for twenty years and he has arrived at a position that satisfies him about eighty per cent of the time.
There were flies.

There must have been flies, and there were probably beetles, and there was something dying in a hole in a field, and a kestrel is an opportunist and will take an insect and will absolutely notice a smell and a movement and a change in a patch of ground.
That is almost certainly all it was.
She was not standing guard.
She was not signalling.
She was a small falcon economically monitoring an anomaly, for four days, at considerable metabolic cost, because there was something in that corner and she had noticed and she is built to notice.
Which is, when he says it out loud, not actually a smaller thing than the version people want.
The dog belonged to a family in Almeirim who had lost her from a car five days earlier and had put up posters in the wrong town.
She lived another nine years.
Tomás is thirty-three.
He does not have a job that has anything to do with birds.

But he has never in his life been able to walk past a hovering kestrel without stopping, and he has twice made himself late for things by standing in a road counting the minutes she stays in one place, and once — only once, in a lay-by on the way to Beja in 2019, over a drainage ditch — it was four days again, and he went and looked, and there was nothing there at all, and he sat back in the car feeling foolish and then, on the whole, not.
